exam_mental.EMD1 2022-2023 Q13: Fructose-6-P has already passed the hexokinase step, so only PFK-1 costs 1 ATP; the payoff phase still gives 4 ATP (reactions 7 and 10, ×2). Going to lactate, the NADH is spent on lactate dehydrogenase, so no respiratory-chain ATP: 4 − 1 = 3 ATP.
exam_mental.EMD1 2023-2024 Q11: Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA by PDH gives 1 NADH = 3 ATP; one Krebs turn gives 12 ATP (3 NADH = 9, 1 FADH₂ = 2, 1 GTP = 1). 3 + 12 = 15 ATP. 2 and 8 are glycolysis values, 12 is acetyl-CoA alone.

questions.stem: About the glycolysis reactions numbered 1 to 5 in the figure:
options: Reaction 1 is catalyzed by hexokinase (or glucokinase in the liver)
Reaction 2 is catalyzed by triose phosphate isomerase
Reaction 3 is catalyzed by phosphofructokinase-1 and irreversibly commits glucose to glycolysis
Reaction 4 is catalyzed by aldolase and cleaves fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into two triose phosphates
questions.explanation: 1 = hexokinase, 2 = phosphohexose isomerase (G6P ⇌ F6P), 3 = PFK-1 (the major, irreversible regulatory step), 4 = aldolase (→ G3P + DHAP), 5 = triose phosphate isomerase. Triose phosphate isomerase acts on trioses, not on G6P.

questions.stem: About the glycolysis reactions numbered 6 to 10 in the figure:
options: Reaction 6 is catalyzed by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and reduces NAD⁺
Reaction 7 is catalyzed by pyruvate kinase
Reaction 9 is catalyzed by enolase and releases water
Reaction 8 is one of the three irreversible steps of glycolysis
questions.explanation: 6 = glyceraldehyde-3-P dehydrogenase (NADH), 7 = phosphoglycerate kinase (1st ATP), 8 = phosphoglycerate mutase (reversible), 9 = enolase (−H₂O), 10 = pyruvate kinase (2nd ATP). The three irreversible steps are 1, 3 and 10.

questions.stem: About the energy balance of glycolysis (glucose → 2 pyruvate):
options: The net gain is 2 ATP per glucose
The 4 ATP formed come from the reactions catalyzed by phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase
Under aerobic conditions the total yield is 8 ATP
Each of the 2 NADH,H⁺ yields 2 ATP in the respiratory chain
questions.explanation: Two reactions consume 1 ATP each (hexokinase, PFK-1) and two produce 2 ATP each (7 and 10): net 2 ATP. Aerobically, the 2 NADH,H⁺ give 3 ATP each (not 2): 2 + 6 = 8 ATP.

questions.stem: Which glycolytic enzymes catalyze irreversible reactions that gluconeogenesis must bypass?
options: Hexokinase (glucokinase)
Phosphoglycerate kinase
Phosphofructokinase-1
Pyruvate kinase
questions.explanation: Steps 1, 3 and 10 (hexokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase) are irreversible and are bypassed by glucose-6-phosphatase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and pyruvate carboxylase + PEPCK. Phosphoglycerate kinase is reversible and shared by both pathways.

questions.stem: The phosphoryl groups carried by glycolytic intermediates:
options: Give them a net negative charge at pH 7, which prevents them from leaving the cell
Allow them to diffuse freely through the plasma membrane into the blood
Are supplied by NADH,H⁺
Act as binding and recognition elements for the enzymes
questions.explanation: The phosphate gives a negative charge (trapping the intermediate inside the cell), conserves energy for ATP synthesis and helps enzyme–substrate recognition. It comes from ATP or Pi, not from NADH.

questions.stem: About the allosteric regulation of phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1):
options: It is activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
It is inhibited by ATP and citrate
It is inhibited by fructose-6-phosphate
It catalyzes the most rate-limiting step of glycolysis
questions.explanation: PFK-1 activators: AMP, ADP, fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, fructose-6-phosphate; inhibitors: ATP, citrate. Fructose-6-phosphate is its substrate and an activator, not an inhibitor.

questions.stem: About the hormonal regulation of glycolysis:
options: After a meal, insulin increases hepatic glucokinase, PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase by activating the transcription of their genes
During fasting, glucagon inhibits glycolysis
Insulin acts mainly by allosteric inhibition of pyruvate kinase
Inhibition of hepatic glycolysis by glucagon spares glucose for glucose-dependent tissues such as the brain and kidneys
questions.explanation: Insulin raises the amounts of the three key enzymes (gene transcription), which speeds glycolysis; glucagon does the opposite and preserves glucose for the brain and kidneys. Insulin is not an allosteric effector — pyruvate kinase is allosterically inhibited by ATP.

questions.stem: During a 100 m sprint, the quadriceps contract intensely with little oxygen. In these muscle cells:
options: The NADH from glycolysis is used to reduce pyruvate to lactate
The reaction is catalyzed by lactate dehydrogenase
The regenerated NAD⁺ is reused by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, so glycolysis can continue
Pyruvate is converted to ethanol by pyruvate decarboxylase
questions.explanation: Without oxygen, cytosolic NADH cannot feed the respiratory chain; lactate dehydrogenase reoxidizes it while reducing pyruvate to lactate, and the NAD⁺ returns to step 6. Pyruvate decarboxylase/alcoholic fermentation is found in yeasts, not in human muscle.

questions.stem: About alcoholic fermentation:
options: It occurs in yeasts and certain microorganisms
Its end product is lactate
It uses pyruvate decarboxylase then alcohol dehydrogenase
It releases CO₂
questions.explanation: In yeasts, pyruvate is decarboxylated (releasing CO₂) then reduced by alcohol dehydrogenase, using NADH: glucose → 2 ethanol + 2 CO₂. Lactate is the product of lactic fermentation.

questions.stem: About pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH):
options: It converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA in the mitochondrion
It requires TPP, lipoic acid, CoA-SH, FAD and NAD⁺ as cofactors
The reaction it catalyzes is reversible
It is inhibited by NADH, acetyl-CoA and ATP
questions.explanation: PDH catalyzes the mitochondrial oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate with five cofactors; it is activated by pyruvate, NAD⁺, CoA-SH, AMP and inhibited by its products NADH, acetyl-CoA and ATP. The reaction is highly exergonic, hence irreversible.

questions.stem: Isolated mitochondria completely oxidize 2 molecules of pyruvate to CO₂ and H₂O. Using the lesson's values (3 ATP/NADH, 2 ATP/FADH₂), how many ATP are produced?
questions.explanation: Per pyruvate: PDH gives 1 NADH (3 ATP) and the Krebs cycle 12 ATP = 15 ATP; for two pyruvates, 30 ATP. 24 is two acetyl-CoA only; 38 includes glycolysis.
questions.mental: Memorise 15 per pyruvate (3 + 12) and double it. Anything ending in the glycolysis portion (38) is excluded because the mitochondria started from pyruvate, not glucose.

questions.stem: About the Krebs cycle:
options: Acetyl-CoA (2 C) condenses with oxaloacetate (4 C) to form citrate (6 C)
It has eight reactions: seven soluble enzymes and one enzyme anchored in the inner mitochondrial membrane
Each turn produces 3 NADH,H⁺ and 1 FADH₂
Two carbons are released as CO₂ per turn, allowing oxaloacetate to be regenerated
questions.explanation: All four are stated on the lesson slide: citrate formation, 8 reactions (succinate dehydrogenase is the membrane-bound one), 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂ per turn, and loss of two carbons as CO₂.

questions.stem: Which Krebs cycle enzymes reduce NAD⁺ to NADH,H⁺?
options: Isocitrate dehydrogenase
α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
Succinate dehydrogenase
Malate dehydrogenase
questions.explanation: The three NADH of the cycle come from isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate, α-ketoglutarate → succinyl-CoA and malate → oxaloacetate. Succinate dehydrogenase uses FAD (→ FADH₂).

questions.stem: About succinate dehydrogenase:
options: It converts succinate into fumarate
Its coenzyme is FAD
It is a soluble enzyme of the mitochondrial matrix
It releases CO₂
questions.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase oxidizes succinate to fumarate, reducing FAD to FADH₂. It is the only Krebs enzyme anchored in the inner mitochondrial membrane; the two CO₂ come from isocitrate and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenases.

questions.stem: A tissue oxidizes 3 molecules of acetyl-CoA through the Krebs cycle and the respiratory chain. How many ATP are formed (lesson values)?
questions.explanation: One turn = 3 NADH (9 ATP) + 1 FADH₂ (2 ATP) + 1 GTP (1 ATP) = 12 ATP; 3 turns = 36 ATP. 45 would be 3 pyruvates (15 each).
questions.mental: 12 per acetyl-CoA × 3 = 36. Don't confuse with 15 per pyruvate (which adds the PDH NADH).

questions.stem: About the regulation of the Krebs cycle:
options: It is inhibited by ATP, NADH and succinyl-CoA
It is activated by ATP and NADH
Citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are its main regulated enzymes
It is regulated mainly by insulin-induced gene transcription
questions.explanation: The cycle follows the energy state: ATP, NADH and succinyl-CoA (high energy) inhibit it; ADP and Ca²⁺ activate it. The three regulated enzymes are citrate synthase, isocitrate DH and α-KG DH. The lesson describes no hormonal transcription control for it.

questions.stem: The Krebs cycle is said to be amphibolic because:
options: It oxidizes acetyl-CoA to produce energy
It supplies intermediates for the synthesis of amino acids, purine bases and heme
It is purely anabolic
It is the main metabolic crossroads between anabolism and catabolism
questions.explanation: Amphibolic = both catabolic (acetyl-CoA oxidation) and anabolic (precursors for biosynthesis); the lesson calls it the principal crossroads of this type. It is not purely anabolic.

questions.stem: About the mitochondrial respiratory chain:
options: It is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane
Complex II is NADH–coenzyme Q oxidoreductase
Coenzyme Q and cytochrome c are mobile electron carriers
Its rate increases rapidly when ADP concentration rises
questions.explanation: Complex I is NADH–CoQ oxidoreductase; complex II is succinate–CoQ oxidoreductase. The chain sits in the inner membrane, uses CoQ and cytochrome c as mobile carriers, and is controlled by ADP concentration.

questions.stem: About the shuttles that transfer cytosolic NADH,H⁺ into the mitochondrion:
options: The glycerol phosphate shuttle operates in muscle and brain and yields 2 ATP per cytosolic NADH
The malate–aspartate shuttle operates in liver, kidneys and heart and yields 3 ATP per cytosolic NADH
Cytosolic NADH itself crosses the inner mitochondrial membrane
Depending on the shuttle, one glucose yields 36 or 38 ATP
questions.explanation: The inner membrane is impermeable to NADH: only its electrons are transferred, either to FAD (glycerol phosphate shuttle → FADH₂ → 2 ATP) or to mitochondrial NADH (malate–aspartate → 3 ATP), hence 36 or 38 ATP per glucose.

questions.stem: A glucose molecule is completely oxidized in a brain cell, where cytosolic NADH enters the mitochondrion by the glycerol phosphate shuttle. ATP yield (lesson values)?
questions.explanation: The total of 38 ATP assumes 3 ATP per glycolytic NADH. With the glycerol phosphate shuttle, each of the 2 cytosolic NADH gives only 2 ATP (via FADH₂): 38 − 2 = 36 ATP.
questions.mental: Start from 38 and subtract 1 ATP for each of the 2 glycolytic NADH (3 → 2): 36. 8 is aerobic glycolysis only.

questions.stem: In a muscle working without oxygen, glucose-1-phosphate released from glycogen is degraded to lactate. What is the ATP yield per glucose-1-phosphate?
options: 2 ATP
3 ATP
4 ATP
5 ATP
questions.explanation: Glucose-1-P → glucose-6-P (phosphoglucomutase) costs no ATP, so the hexokinase step is skipped: only PFK-1 consumes 1 ATP, and the payoff phase still yields 4 ATP: 4 − 1 = 3 ATP. The NADH is used by lactate dehydrogenase, so it gives no ATP.
questions.mental: Free glucose: −2 + 4 = 2. Entering as glucose-1-P or glucose-6-P saves the hexokinase ATP: 3. Anaerobic → no NADH ATP.

questions.stem: About the enzymes in the green boxes of the figure:
options: They bypass the three irreversible reactions of glycolysis
They are all cytosolic
PEP carboxykinase consumes ATP
Pyruvate carboxylase requires biotin (vitamin B8)
questions.explanation: Pyruvate carboxylase (mitochondrial, biotin, 1 ATP) + PEPCK (1 GTP), fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase replace pyruvate kinase, PFK-1 and hexokinase. Pyruvate carboxylase is strictly mitochondrial, and PEPCK uses GTP, not ATP.

questions.stem: About gluconeogenesis in humans:
options: About 90% of new glucose is made in the liver, 10% in the kidneys and intestinal epithelium
It does not occur in muscle or brain
It consumes 2 ATP per glucose formed from 2 pyruvates
Its first reaction, pyruvate → oxaloacetate, takes place in the cytosol
questions.explanation: Gluconeogenesis costs 6 ATP equivalents per glucose (4 ATP + 2 GTP) — three times the 2 ATP gained by glycolysis. Pyruvate is carboxylated inside the mitochondrial matrix by pyruvate carboxylase.

questions.stem: About gluconeogenic precursors and their entry points:
options: Glycerol enters at dihydroxyacetone phosphate
Lactate and alanine enter at pyruvate
Even-chain fatty acids enter via acetyl-CoA
Propionate enters via succinyl-CoA, then proceeds toward phosphoenolpyruvate
questions.explanation: Entry points: pyruvate (lactate, alanine), PEP via Krebs intermediates (glucogenic amino acids, propionate from odd-chain fatty acids), DHAP (glycerol). In humans acetyl-CoA cannot be converted into glucose, so fatty acids are not gluconeogenic.

questions.stem: On the third day of a fast, which cycle supplies the liver with a constant gluconeogenic precursor derived from muscle proteins?
options: The Cori cycle
The Felig (glucose–alanine) cycle
The Krebs cycle
The pentose phosphate pathway
questions.explanation: During prolonged fasting, muscle protein catabolism (and glycolytic pyruvate) gives alanine, which travels to the liver and is reconverted to pyruvate → glucose: the Felig cycle. The Cori cycle recycles lactate from anaerobic muscle.

questions.stem: About the hormonal regulation of gluconeogenesis:
options: Glucagon induces the synthesis of PEP carboxykinase and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
Insulin slows gluconeogenesis after a meal
Glucagon activates glycolysis
Glucagon is secreted when blood glucose falls between meals
questions.explanation: Fasting → low glycemia → glucagon, which accelerates gluconeogenesis (inducing PEPCK and F1,6BPase) and inhibits glycolysis. Insulin has the opposite effects after a meal.

questions.stem: About the pentose phosphate pathway:
options: It occurs in the cytosol
It produces no ATP
It operates only in the liver
It produces erythrose-4-phosphate, a precursor of aromatic amino acids
questions.explanation: The PPP is cytosolic and ubiquitous (activity varies with the need for NADPH and ribose), generates no energy, and yields NADPH, ribose-5-P and erythrose-4-P (→ tyrosine, tryptophan, phenylalanine).

questions.stem: About the pathway shown in the figure:
options: NADH,H⁺ is produced at two steps of its oxidative phase
One CO₂ is released, by 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase
The reactions of its non-oxidative phase are irreversible
Its end products, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and fructose-6-phosphate, can enter glycolysis
questions.explanation: The oxidative phase produces 2 NADPH (not NADH) at G6PD and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase, the latter also releasing the only CO₂. The non-oxidative phase is reversible and regulated by substrate availability.

questions.stem: A boy develops acute hemolytic anemia a few hours after eating fava beans. About this condition:
options: It results from a glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, which lowers NADPH production
Oxidized glutathione (GS–SG) can no longer be efficiently reduced back to GSH
Peroxides accumulate and oxidize hemoglobin Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺
A similar crisis can follow intake of drugs such as aspirin or sulfonamides
questions.explanation: Favism: G6PD deficiency → less NADPH → reduced glutathione is not regenerated → peroxides deform the red-cell membrane and oxidize hemoglobin. Oxidizing drugs (aspirin, sulfonamides) trigger the same crisis.

questions.stem: In the pathway shown, congenital galactosemia is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme that catalyzes:
options: Galactose → galactose-1-phosphate
Galactose-1-phosphate + UDP-glucose → glucose-1-phosphate + UDP-galactose
Glucose-1-phosphate → glucose-6-phosphate
UDP-galactose ⇌ UDP-glucose
questions.explanation: Classic galactosemia is a galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency. Galactokinase catalyzes A, phosphoglucomutase C and UDP-hexose 4-epimerase D.

questions.stem: About congenital galactosemia:
options: Cataracts result from galactitol, formed from galactose by aldose reductase
Cataracts result from sorbitol formed from galactose
The body cannot synthesize galactose, so it must stay in the diet
It is the most common inherited disorder of carbohydrate metabolism
questions.explanation: Accumulated galactose is reduced by aldose reductase to galactitol, which opacifies the lens; sorbitol comes from glucose (cataracts in diabetics). A galactose-free diet prevents the disease, because the body can make galactose from glucose.

questions.stem: Hereditary fructose intolerance, with accumulation of fructose-1-phosphate, hypoglycemia and vomiting, is due to a deficiency of:
options: Hepatic fructokinase
Aldolase B
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Hexokinase
questions.explanation: Aldolase B deficiency blocks fructose-1-phosphate cleavage → hereditary fructose intolerance. Fructokinase deficiency gives essential fructosuria, which is benign and asymptomatic.

questions.stem: About glycogen synthesis:
options: The liver stores about 150 g of glycogen, one-third of the body's total
The branching enzyme transfers a fragment of 7 glucose residues to form an α(1→6) linkage
Its key enzyme is glycogen phosphorylase
It is stimulated by glucagon
questions.explanation: Liver ≈ 150 g (1/3), muscle ≈ 300 g (2/3). Glycogen synthase is the key enzyme of synthesis, stimulated by insulin; glycogen phosphorylase degrades glycogen under glucagon/epinephrine.

questions.stem: About hepatic and muscle glycogen:
options: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so its glycogen is for "private use"
The hepatic glycogen store can be depleted within about 24 hours
Epinephrine stimulates muscle glycogenolysis during exercise
Muscle glycogen directly maintains blood glucose during fasting
questions.explanation: Only the liver has glucose-6-phosphatase and can export free glucose ("public use"); muscle G6P stays in the cell for glycolysis. Hepatic glycogen lasts ≈ 24 h; glucagon (liver) and epinephrine (muscle) trigger glycogenolysis.

questions.stem: Von Gierke disease (type I glycogen storage disease: severe hypoglycemia, big liver, lactic acidosis) is due to a deficiency of:
options: Glucose-6-phosphatase
Muscle glycogen phosphorylase
Lysosomal α1,4-glucosidase
The branching enzyme
questions.explanation: Type I (Von Gierke) = glucose-6-phosphatase: the liver cannot release glucose. Muscle phosphorylase = McArdle (V), lysosomal α1,4-glucosidase = Pompe (II), branching enzyme = Andersen (IV).

questions.stem: About intestinal absorption of monosaccharides:
options: At the apical membrane, SGLT1 co-transports glucose and galactose with Na⁺
GLUT2 mediates fructose entry at the apical membrane
At the basolateral membrane, GLUT2 releases glucose, fructose and galactose into the blood
SGLT transporters work by passive facilitated diffusion
questions.explanation: Apical: SGLT1 (glucose, galactose, Na⁺; secondary active transport driven by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase gradient) and GLUT5 (fructose). Basolateral: GLUT2 for all three. GLUTs, not SGLTs, work by facilitated diffusion.

questions.stem: About the digestion of dietary carbohydrates:
options: Salivary α-amylase randomly cleaves α-1,4-glycosidic bonds of starch
Amylase digestion continues actively in the stomach
Lactose digestion is a rate-limiting step because lactase acts slowly
Cellulose is not digested and is part of dietary fiber
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase starts starch hydrolysis but is inactivated by the gastric acid, so no carbohydrate digestion occurs in the stomach. Lactase (β-galactosidase) is slower than sucrase; cellulose is undigested fiber.
